patches.old: Choice B is a common error if students mistakenly add only the exponents they observe without correctly identifying the order with respect to B.
patches.new: Choice B is the common error: students read 27 = 3³ correctly, conclude third order in B, and then report that number as the overall order — forgetting to add the first-order dependence on A. The overall order is always the sum of the individual orders.
patches.reason: The stated route to choice B does not produce choice B. "Adding only the exponents they observe" is the correct procedure (1 + 3 = 4), so as written the distractor rationale describes the right method and attributes the wrong answer to it. The actual route to 3 is identifying the order in B correctly and then failing to add the order in A, which is the error worth naming.

sources.title: OpenStax, Chemistry 2e — Kinetics (chapter 12 summary)
sources.note: Rate laws are determined experimentally and cannot be predicted from reaction stoichiometry; the overall order of a reaction is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant. Unimolecular elementary steps are first order, bimolecular elementary steps second order.

sources.title: Chemistry LibreTexts (OpenStax Chemistry 2e) — 12.4 Integrated Rate Laws
sources.note: Integrated forms and linear diagnostic plots: [A] vs t for zero order (slope −k), ln[A] vs t for first order (slope −k), 1/[A] vs t for second order (slope +k); half-lives [A]0/2k, 0.693/k and 1/(k[A]0) respectively.

visual.title: Three orders, three signatures
visual.alt: A concentration-against-time plot showing zero-, first- and second-order decay from the same starting concentration: the zero-order line is straight and reaches zero at a definite time, the first-order curve is exponential and halves in equal steps, and the second-order curve falls steeply then develops a long tail. Below, one panel per order gives the rate law, the integrated form, the plot that comes out straight, the half-life and whether it shortens, stays constant or lengthens, the units of k, and a worked example of where that order shows up. Two footers cover how to read a rate law from a table or a mechanism, and what changes k — temperature and activation energy through the Arrhenius equation, and a catalyst, which lowers the barrier in both directions and so changes neither the free energy change nor the equilibrium constant.
visual.caption: Identify the order first: the integrated form, the straight-line plot, the half-life behaviour and the units of k all follow from it.
